newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Norwich plans flotation to unlock value.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norwich plans flotation to unlock value.

text.p: Norwich Union Life Insurance Society said on Wednesday it is planning the first stock market flotation by a mutually-owned British insurance company, which will give shares to nearly three million members.
It plans to float on the London Stock Exchange, creating a new holding company, Norwich Union Plc, in a move likely to be worth between 4.0 billion and 4.5 billion pounds ($6.26-$7.05 billion).
Chief executive Allan Bridgewater said the flotation will unlock value for policy holders and enable it to expand to meet increased opportunities.
"This is a good news day for members of Norwich Union," Bridgewater told Reuters. "The current structure is no longer appropriate and the flotation will unlock hidden value."

However, Bridgewater and chairman George Paul declined to comment on the likely valuation of the company when floated or on the value of policyholders' free shares entitlements, which press reports suggest will be 500-700 pounds for most people.
"We're not prepared to comment on the amount of capital to be raised," he told a news conference, adding that details would be made available next spring.
Norwich Union is one of the country's largest insurance groups with funds under management of about 40 billion pounds and worldwide gross premium income of 4.7 billion last year.
Qualifying members will receive free shares in Norwich Union Plc and preferential rights to subscribe cash for further shares but the door for new members will be closed from today, it said.
In a move aimed at heading off any suggestion that the directors may have taken the decision in their own interests, Bridgewater said they would not be entitled to any extra shares.
"The board took this decision because we are concerned to avoid any idea that directors will benefit," he told reporters.
Investment analysts said the valuation figure of 4.0-4.5 billion was probably about right. "It doesn't look unreasonable to me," said Lehman Brothers analyst Rob Procter.

Another analyst said the lack of information about the value of Norwich Union's various businesses would reduce the likelihood of a hostile takeover bid before trading begins in Norwich Union shares, probabbly in the summer of 1997.
The Norwich has more than five million customers worldwide of whom about three million are members of the society.

Most holders of existing life, pensions and annuity policies of the society are members, which includes holders of policies issued by its overseas operations. The group earned around 28 percent of its 1995 gross written premiums outside Britain.
But holders of motor, household and healthcare policies will not receive the share windfall.
Bridgewater said the company's life fund will receive a major capital injection and members will get shares in the new company representing the hidden value.

He explained that, under its current structure, the life fund is the owner of all of its businesses including its general insurance operations. This has had implications for the company which include restrictions on it ability to access capital.
After the flotation, Norwich Union Plc will have two new life insurance units with the rest of the business held outside the life fund.
Bridgewater said Norwich Union was well placed to exploit the expected large expansion of the pensions industry in the next decade.
He said governments around Europe were moving towards the encouragement of personal provision of pensions and that this represented a big opportunity.

Asked if he was concerned that Britain's largest banks were busily moving into the life and pensions market, Bridgewater said, "I suspect no bank can point to a track record or a market position like ours."
Equally, although Norwich provides some mortgages already, Bridgewater said it was not likely to move aggressively for market share in that area.
He said that the company had moved recently to reinforce the management of its asset management business and said that this expertise would be extended.
Bridgewater said Norwich Union had no plans to make acquisitions but did not go as far as ruling them out.
"We are already a major player," he said. "We have no laid out plans for acquisitions."
